items.description_html:
India Is Betting Billions on Lithium-Ion. What If the Next Battery Revolution Moves Beyond It?

Everyone is chasing EV batteries. But the next big demand could come from AI, robotics, defence and power grids.

Barclays Research highlights a major shift:

🔹 Lithium-ion: EVs and energy storage
🔹 Solid-state: Premium EVs and robots
🔹 Sodium-ion: Low-cost mobility and grid storage
🔹 Flow & metal-air: Long-duration power backup
🔹 Lithium-sulfur: Drones and defence

The India angle?

We are building battery gigafactories while tomorrow's industries may demand very different technologies.
Lithium-ion isn't disappearing. But it may not capture every new opportunity.

The next battery multibagger may not be the company making the most batteries, but the one making the right batteries.

Are Indian investors looking beyond the EV hype?

items.title: America Has Oil. So Why Is Its Top Diplomat Flying to a Refinery in Gujarat? That's the surprise in the global energy crisis. 🇺🇸 US Secretary of...
items.description_html:
America Has Oil. So Why Is Its Top Diplomat Flying to a Refinery in Gujarat?

That's the surprise in the global energy crisis.

🇺🇸 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is heading to Reliance's Jamnagar refinery.

His agenda? Get Reliance to refine more Venezuelan crude and explore oil production in Venezuela.

Now connect this with Morgan Stanley's latest research.

The global oil bottleneck is shifting from crude availability to refining capacity, particularly diesel.

🇳🇱 Netherlands: Imports crude, exports refined fuels.

🇮🇳 India: Imports nearly 90% of its crude, yet exports diesel.

🇪🇺 Europe: Remains structurally dependent on imported diesel.

The irony? America is looking to an Indian refinery to help address global energy security.

And here lies India's opportunity.

Higher crude prices can hurt our economy, while stronger diesel refining margins could benefit companies like Reliance.

Oil reserves create geopolitical power. Refining capacity may increasingly determine who captures the profits.

Rubio's Jamnagar visit is more than diplomacy. It's a reminder of how strategically important India's refining industry has become.

items.description_html:
The Next Power Sector Multibagger May Not Be a Solar Company.

India's Power Paradox: 56% Non-Fossil Capacity. Just 20% Renewable Electricity.

India's energy transition is accelerating. But the numbers reveal a fascinating disconnect.

⚡ Non-fossil capacity has jumped from 33% in FY17 to 56% in FY27 YTD.

☀️ Solar capacity has surged nearly 14x, from 12 GW to 171 GW.

📈 Renewable capacity additions hit a record 50.8 GW in FY26, versus just 11.8 GW in FY18.

Yet renewables generated only 17% of electricity in FY26, rising to around 20% in FY27 YTD.

The next big beneficiaries could be battery storage, pumped hydro, transmission infrastructure, grid equipment and flexible power generation.

Between January 2025 and October 2026, Trump's administration generated 749 recorded tariff-rate statements, covering threats, announcements, implemented tariffs and repeated references to existing measures.

Strip out the repetitions, and the dataset counts 341 distinct tariff measures.

items.title: Both Bounce and Yulu started out in 2017-18 building micro-mobility solutions for urban consumers, as startups like Bird in the US and Ofo in China we...
items.description_html:
Both Bounce and Yulu started out in 2017-18 building micro-mobility solutions for urban consumers, as startups like Bird in the US and Ofo in China were becoming big.

But the Covid-19 lockdown forced both companies to rethink their models and start catering to gig workers and hyperlocal delivery platforms.

Today, their core business is renting electric vehicles to gig workers.

The number of active riders across just Eternal (Zomato and Blinkit) and Swiggy has increased nearly 3x over the past five years from 350,000-400,000 to about 1.1 million active riders a month.

Yulu was the first to pivot towards gig workers.

It worked with original equipment manufacturers such as Bajaj, which is also a shareholder, to develop low-speed electric vehicles. These are particularly suited for quick commerce, which now accounts for about 60% of Yulu’s business.

Bounce took a different route. It entered manufacturing directly by acquiring 22Motors and built an electric scooter that can also handle longer commutes, making it suitable for use cases such as bike taxis and courier services.

Now, Yulu has also entered this segment with a new vehicle of its own.

@thearc_hq has a deep dive on both companies, how their models have evolved, and the strategies they are betting on next.

items.title: RT Turner Novak 🍌🧢: Ken Griffin says AI is "almost certainly" in a bubble. Back in 2024, @loganbartlett of @Redpoint told me how VCs actually pl...
items.description_html:
RT Turner Novak 🍌🧢
Ken Griffin says AI is "almost certainly" in a bubble.

Back in 2024, @loganbartlett of @Redpoint told me how VCs actually play bubbles:

"From a pure incentive standpoint, your job would be to lean into it. Raise as much as you can, deploy as much as you can.

If you're right, you get to say, 'I told you so.' If you're wrong, you justify it as the mania of the markets. You hope enough people did it that it's forgivable.

That's what happened with the internet in '99, 2000, 2001. That's what happened with crypto. And it feels like that's what's happening with AI in some ways as well.

If everyone is saying something is true, and it's getting covered on CNBC on a daily basis, it's generally something I want to stay away from.

But bubbles lay infrastructure for enabling technologies. The internet was a bubble, and no one would argue it wasn't ultimately correct. It just wasn't a great investment at the time.

If you were in Google, eBay, PayPal, Amazon, you did very well. If you were in Lycos or Ask Jeeves or Friendster, you got totally wiped out.

Just because you're right on the tech doesn't mean you're right on the opportunity."


Polymarket: JUST IN: Citadel’s Ken Griffin warns AI is “almost certainly” in a bubble right now.

items.title: RT Sajith Pai: Really enjoyed this interview (a little dated; from Jan26) of @Kanwal_fireside w @madhavchanchani of @thearc_hq - the whole interview i...
items.description_html:
RT Sajith Pai
Really enjoyed this interview (a little dated; from Jan26) of @Kanwal_fireside w @madhavchanchani of @thearc_hq - the whole interview is worth a read, especially useful to understand how they have built the fund to deliver returns (and amongst the highest in the Indian fundscape) without adopting a power law approach.

V interesting points (useful to consumer brands founders) on what acquirers look for: one key point is that they dont like companies w high SKU sprawl. They love companies w 1-2 hero SKUs (easier to integrate into their sales machine + supply chain).

The other one was on how Marico has housed its acquisitions under a diff division, to ensure they dont lose the insurgent energy. Marico is a great example of how a FMCG major has cleverly used M&A to grow. Claude tells me "The acquired businesses (Beardo, 4700BC, Cosmix, True Elements, Plix) brought in a combined ₹2,375 crore in FY26, against total revenue of ₹13,611 crore. That works out to about 17.5% of consolidated revenue."

Definitely the synergies w @sharrpventures and Rishabh's deep understanding of the consumer brands / DTC startup space helps Marico.

items.description_html:
RT Pratik Bhakta
Dezerv is playing the long-term wealth game, focusing on the newly-rich Indians.

In a crowded wealthtech market, Dezerv’s mutual fund PMF approach is trying to create a differentiated use case for this user base.

It has raised $100mn, has built a significantly large AUM base and some loyal customers too.

But this business has two major challenges:

1. Scaling: A RM-dependent business means there cannot be a sudden quick scale up.

2. Retention of acquired customers.

Dezerv understands these challenges and they have their own plans around dealing with them.
